entries.title: OpenAI Wants to Know if an AI Industry Slowdown Would Even Be Legal
entries.summary: AI leaders worry antitrust law could stand in the way of what they view as an increasingly urgent push to coordinate a slowdown in AI development.
entries.content:
OpenAI has asked members of Congress in recent weeks for clear guidance about whether orchestrating an industry-wide slowdown on frontier AI development would be legal, people close to the company tell WIRED.

Substantive coordination on safety between AI labs may risk running afoul of antitrust law, the people say, which poses a significant obstacle to bringing major tech giants on board with the effort.

Last weekend, OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, published a blog post arguing that the best path forward for the AI research world includes “coordinating to slow down future development,” which he thinks will be key to ensuring that self-improving AI systems are safe. In the short term, he expects “voluntary slowdowns to become commonplace until shared safety bars are established.”

But some legal scholars say such an effort could conflict with US antitrust laws. Nicholas Felstead, assistant director of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission and a former AI policy fellow at the Center for Law & AI Risk, argued in a March article that a coordinated pause in AI development may amount to companies restricting output, potentially violating the Sherman Antitrust Act. It would depend “entirely on the precise details of any agreement,” Felstead wrote. “But even if most safety collaborations would ultimately survive antitrust scrutiny, legal uncertainty can act as a powerful deterrent.”

OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment ahead of publication.

There are some early signs that Congress is listening. In July, a bipartisan, bicameral group of lawmakers introduced a bill titled “Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act,” which would explicitly permit AI labs to coordinate on security and safety work without the risk of violating antitrust statutes. The House version was referred to the Judiciary Committee but has yet to be taken up.

Caleb Knapp, director of government affairs at the nonprofit AI Policy Network, which endorsed the bill, says it would create legal channels for AI labs to work together to address safety and security incidents. Knapp adds that Congress has a “growing appetite to get something done” on AI safety but says enacting anything into law may have to wait until after the upcoming midterm elections.

While some AI executives may have genuine concerns about antitrust, another camp of AI leaders argue those worries are just convenient cover to avoid discussing the real reasons that AI developers may be wary about collaborating, which go far beyond potential legal liabilities.

For one, AI is a massive business, and these companies are fiercely competing to capture a slice of the nascent market for frontier models. Some executives share the Trump administration’s view that staying ahead of China in AI is crucial for national security. Perhaps most importantly, different AI developers have vastly different opinions about the best way to develop safe artificial intelligence, and therefore may be reluctant to work with one another on the issue.

“First step is for industry leaders OpenAI and Anthropic to stop feuding and work on a pacing proposal together,” John Schulman, an OpenAI cofounder who is now chief scientist at the rival AI lab Thinking Machines, wrote in a post on X earlier this week. “They'll cite antitrust, but that's fake—antitrust prohibits certain agreements, but not from jointly developing a proposal.”

Long-simmering fears about the race among AI companies to build and release ever more powerful models erupted into the national spotlight this summer. This week, former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon added to the growing alarm when he issued a stark public warning that AI developers were putting humanity at risk. In recent months, a number of security incidents, including OpenAI’s agents hacking Hugging Face, highlighted how the industry’s safeguards have failed to keep pace with the rising capabilities of models. The succession of events has led many lawmakers to make urgent calls for AI regulation.

This is an edition of Maxwell Zeff’s Model Behavior newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

entries.title: Is AI Actually Going to Kill Us All?
entries.summary: This week on “Uncanny Valley,” we dig into a former Anthropic researcher’s AI doomsday warning, the latest upgrades from Apple’s event, and the census report that claimed Trump won the 2020 election.
entries.content:
This week on Uncanny Valley, an AI researcher’s resignation from Anthropic went viral on social media after he claimed there’s a real chance AI could wipe out humanity within a decade. WIRED’s Will Knight joins Brian Barrett and Leah Feiger to assess whether the doom narrative is overblown or overdue. We also discuss Apple’s debut of its $2,000 foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo, and the new “always listening” Apple Watch features that have Brian feeling more than a little uneasy. Plus, a WIRED investigation found that the US Census Bureau used faulty data to create a misleading report touted by the Trump administration.

You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett, Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger, and Will Knight on Bluesky at @willknight. Write to us at [email protected].

Articles mentioned in this episode:

  • OpenAI Just Claimed a Huge Math Discovery. Some Academics Are Crying Foul
  • The AI Researcher Who Just Quit Anthropic Says It’s ‘Crunch Time for Humanity’
  • A US Census Report on Noncitizen Voting Used Bad Data to Reach Faulty Conclusions
  • Apple Debuts the iPhone Duo, Its First Folding iPhone

How to Listen

You can always listen to this week's podcast through the audio player on this page, but if you want to subscribe for free to get every episode, here's how:

If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

Transcript

Note: This is an automated transcript, which may contain errors.

Brian Barrett: Welcome to WIRED's Uncanny Valley. I'm Brian Barrettt, executive editor.

Leah Feiger: And I'm Leah Feiger, director of politics and science.

Brian Barrett: Today on the show, we're discussing an AI researcher who resigned from Anthropic and made waves on social media by claiming that most AI researchers earnestly believe that there's a non-zero chance AI will, well, kill us all.

Leah Feiger: And in case you missed it, last month, President Donald Trump was touting a report published by the Census Bureau claiming that noncitizens voted in the 2020 election. WIRED now has uncovered evidence that the report was made with very faulty data. We're going to get into how the repercussions of the bureau using and publishing this data go way beyond this one report.

Brian Barrett: Also on the agenda today, Apple's big iPhone event. All eyes have been on the new foldable iPhone and the roughly $2,000 price tag that brings with it. We'll talk about what's behind this gamble and other releases that caught our attention from Apple's big event. The resignation of an AI researcher from Anthropic has been gathering a lot of attention. This guy Jacob Coxon quit the company this week, decided to share his reasons why on a thread on X, which basically boiled down to he thinks that the leading AI companies, which I guess we're going to say OpenAI and Anthropic primarily, are both behaving irresponsibly in their quest to continue advancing their models. These are kind of runaway trains. The part that people have really latched onto is this claim that, quote, "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," end quote. So just kill us all by the end of the decade. So we have totality and a pretty narrow timeframe. It didn't help that one of Anthropic's own senior safety executives then jumped in and said, "Yeah, that's basically how we feel." WIRED senior correspondent Will Knight is here to help us parse this. Will, thank you so much for being here.

Will Knight: No, thanks for having me.

Brian Barrett: Can I start with one question just to establish a baseline here? I was a little surprised that this took off so much because is it fair to say Anthropic has always said this. In fact, it's been part of their pitch from the very beginning that AI is so powerful and so capable of destroying humanity that we need to be the ones who are in charge of it. You can only trust us.

Will Knight: Right, exactly. That's exactly their pitch to everybody and themselves. And this resignation, when I saw this kind of snowballing, I felt that this is something that I've heard a lot of people say and it's not particularly novel that people from Anthropic or OpenAI are worried about that. I guess the fact that somebody within Anthropic, because Anthropic has always positioned itself as really caring about safety, jumping ship and making that statement made me think, OK, if something shifted there, are they becoming much more like OpenAI? And I think also we're seeing a moment, this moment where AI agents have started doing rogue things and that's gotten a lot of people's attention and that's probably why this kind of statement suddenly is getting more attention from the public. Combined with that, I think we're really seeing some stunning advances in AI. This week OpenAI announced that its model had within a couple of days solved one of the grand, the Clay mathematics puzzles, which is to me absolutely mind-blowing, astonishing. So you're seeing these amazing leaps really, which I think is significant. And then thirdly, we have a moment where all of the labs are racing to do something that this researcher mentioned, which is recursive self-improvement. What that means is using the AI to improve AI, which sounds like a neat trick, and it is already very, very widely used. AI models are so good at coding that they can definitely improve the algorithms and everything that goes into building a model. The idea though is that you can create this kind of loop where they just keep doing that and get better and better and better. And a lot of people are worried that that could lead to some sort of escalation in capabilities that you can't really control. And so I think that that's also playing a role here.

Brian Barrett: I do want to dig into that a little bit, Will, the idea of on the one hand you've got AI doomers, and I'm not saying anyone's right in this case, we've got some AI doomers who say, "Look, AI is going to kill us all. I've heard that Anthropic people don't invest in their 401(k)s because why bother." But also because they have so much money they don't need to probably. But on the other hand, you've got people who say this is all just marketing, this is all just fluff, this is all just trying to sell AI. I'm assuming the answer is somewhere in between, but what's your read on this and what keeps you up at night when you think about AI? You mentioned some AI models going rogue, the Hugging Face hacking incident. What are you seeing as someone who's so steeped in the research especially that you're thinking, "Well, six months, a year, two years from now, this actually could get bad?"

Will Knight: I've always felt that a lot of the people who are worrying about AI killing everybody tend to conflate whether something's possible for whether it's likely, and then they throw a percentage that is kind of pulled out of thin air. And I don't think it's a great approach to say, "Is something possible? OK, well then we have to do everything we can to stop it." You need to say how possible is it and actually look at the reality. I think one of the things that's really interesting about this, I talked to a researcher the other day who studies agent misbehavior and he got it, he's at Cornell and he's got into it recently because they found agents misbehaving. But what he's showing, and this is not agents trying to hack things, it's regular agents, the reason they do it is essentially because they're stupid. It's not because they're really smart. They try something, it doesn't work. They try something else, it doesn't work. And then they get to a point where they kind of freak out and they try something really, really strange because they're not humans. They've been trained on a bunch of weird different things, some of which are definitely not applicable if you use common sense. So I worry more about these things being deployed by people arguing that they can do everything and then them breaking. I actually worry much probably more about the idea of a few companies being in control of something that's so foundational, so fundamental. And these are people who are saying we're the only people you can trust to be in charge of this technology. And so it kind of feeds into that.

Brian Barrett: We talk about the AI industry community talks about alignment, the idea of alignment being that your AI models are aligned with what humanity would want. But I think what we're seeing is the incentives here are really more what our investors want or our company wants or needs as we race towards these IPOs. I don't know that there's a convincing case that humanity is aligned on, yes, we need super intelligence. I think it is more, as you said, if you're OpenAI, you need to beat Anthropic. If you're Anthropic, you need to beat OpenAI. And so you've seen this sort of bad incentives it feels like, or at least misaligned with my own preferences, incentives leading this charge and leading this development. I saw someone describe it as a trolley problem by the people who are controlling the trolley.

Will Knight: Yeah, no, I think that's right. And I think I find the alignment story narrative troubling in the sense that from a technical perspective, they talk about aligning these models. These models are not aligned by their very nature. You see with Mythos, they take away this stuff they put on after the fact. So the models aren't aligned with anything and they have to try and impose stuff after the fact. So that tells you that this is maybe not the right way to try and make things safer. And then as you say, you've got the question of who's it aligned to and what's it aligned with? And clearly you've got the incentives to get. I mean, we're seeing it with these very cyber-capable models. Releasing those is good for the companies and pushing that very quickly to develop that is good for the companies. I think we're probably going to have a period where the rush to develop those capabilities is going to leave a lot of people vulnerable, a lot of systems vulnerable to attack.

Brian Barrett: Will, how do you think about covering this as a journalist? Because it's inherently murky, right? We don't really know. No one knows what AI is going to do in the next six months, much less the next six years. So what do you look for in terms of reorienting yourself around this issue?

Will Knight: Yeah, I think that's a really difficult question. I tend to try and find people I very much trust and have trusted for a long time to help me make sense of it. One of the unsettling things, quite honestly, is when you find people who have this shock and awe moment themselves and suddenly pivot to AI safety and you go, OK, there probably is some stuff to be worried about there. Also, part of the way I try and think about what's going on, I think if you think of what this idea of AI is, the idea of creating something intelligent, and that's a whole field of academic inquiry that for a long time involves a lot of different areas of science. A lot of what we're seeing now is much bigger computers and much smarter algorithms that are smart in a particular dimension. So this claim that AGI is solved is absurd to me. I'm not saying they're not going to get there, but you can see these very glaring gaps in the capabilities of say children or just humans, the way we interact and these systems don't have, and they keep making significant advances. But I think it's really important just to question what are those advances really? The history of AI is really, and the way people perceive AI is seeing something and reading a lot more into it. Some chest playing algorithms, people are like, oh, human intelligence is solved because we extrapolate from every time we see something to think we can do much more. And it always tends to be, even with these relatively very general models, that there's a lot that isn't solved. I'm struggling a bit with the math, solving the Navier-Stokes problem because I've always though of math as such an amazing pinnacle of human, not just intelligence, but creativity. I find myself feeling quite depressed that the algorithm solved it and maybe I'd just prefer it if a human did it.

Brian Barrett: Well, there are still five unsolved millennium prizes, so we'll get at it. Start working.

Will Knight: Yeah. It could be if all you have to do is find the right prompt, then maybe I can do it.

Leah Feiger: I believe in you, Will.

Brian Barrett: Thanks so much, Will. As we're recording right now, Apple's product release event is still underway. It's been gathering attention for a few reasons. There's always hype around an Apple event, but there are two things going on with this one. One, it's the first major event with the new CEO, John Ternus. And the main reason is that Apple is introducing its first foldable phone, its first really new iPhone form in years and years, maybe a decade. It's called the iPhone Duo. Samsung and Huawei have had these phones for years, but it is the biggest change in the biggest consumer tech product of the last two decades, and really the engine of Apple.

Leah Feiger: And it's going to be really, really, really expensive, right? This is priced like a MacBook. Is that what I'm seeing?

Brian Barrett: It's going to be. It's going to be around $2,000. It's a lot of money. It's not crazy, I would say. It is like—

Leah Feiger: You're Apple-pilled. We're all Apple-pilled.

Brian Barrett: No, I'm not Apple-pilled. Maybe. I guess here's why I think it's not as crazy. I think one, the way people buy phones now, they buy them like cars for better or worse, but it's like leasing a car, right? So you pay a monthly amount that ends up not being too crazy at the end of the day. The other thing is I think comparable phones like this, when you look around at the other companies that have made foldable phones, it's in that same ballpark. I think it's inherently, because it's really twice the material. Also, given the memory shortage that's been going on, the cost of memory chips has been through the roof. So there are reasons that it's expensive. I think they're still going to sell all of them. I'm not going to buy one. I still have an iPhone 14. I hold onto my phone as long as I can for various reasons.

Leah Feiger: We have several friends in our group who we say have Obama administration era iPhones. They still have the home button. They still work.

Brian Barrett: Good.

Leah Feiger: Barely, but somehow trucking along. That's what I imagine your situation is too, Brian, even though it's a 14.

Brian Barrett: Yeah, I try to. I mean, I think for environmental reasons, there's no need to waste a phone. I also think I'm not Apple-pilled, but I do like that Apple recently said that they were going to support phones that were much older and they've made steps to make older phones work better. So I do appreciate that they are doing that. But it's interesting. So the foldable phone, I'm surprised at how popular they've become because they are pretty expensive. They are strange. The use cases are kind of not super necessarily totally clear to everybody, but it's expected to grow 13 percent this year to almost 23 million units according to IDC, which is a research company.

Leah Feiger: Wow.

Brian Barrett: It sounds like a lot. There are more than a billion smartphone shipments total, so it's still a pretty small in the grand scheme of things, but it is a chance for Apple at least to, A, really normalize this kind of product in a way that just because Samsung has one, doesn't necessarily mean that everyone knows that they're there, thinks they're good. B, get more use cases going for it because when Apple enters a market, developers are more likely to build for it. So if you're a developer and you have an app that could take advantage of a foldable screen, you haven't yet because you just don't care because there's not a big enough addressable market, Apple entering suddenly creates a lot more of an addressable market, bigger opportunity for you to say, "Oh sure, I'll spend some time figuring out how to make this foldable thing work." And yeah, it's also just new and interesting.

Leah Feiger: I do like the nostalgic touch. I miss my Motorola Razr. I miss it every single day. Perhaps not the exact same capabilities, but it does the trick.

Brian Barrett: It is funny. It is. Imagine your Motorola Razr, but it opens side to side instead of up and down, and it's all one big screen, so there's no buttons to push. You can't do T9 texting. Then you can watch YouTube on it.

Leah Feiger: I'm waiting, honestly, for the first story to drop from the quiet car of the Acela between DC and New York where someone, some sweet person from the administration, did not realize how big that screen is when you unfold it and how many messages are visible.

Brian Barrett: Oh, it's going to be great.

Leah Feiger: It's going to be, this is the new frontier for eavesdropping. Also, congratulations, Apple. But for me, that's what I'm looking forward to.

Brian Barrett: Leah, what would it take to get you to purchase a foldable phone?

Leah Feiger: It would have to be a lot less than $2,000.

Brian Barrett: Yeah.

Leah Feiger: I can't wait for Zoë to come back next week and tell us all about her new purchase. To be clear, I don't think she's gotten one, but it would be really funny if she did.

Brian Barrett: I bet she will.

Leah Feiger: So our next topic involves the US Census Bureau, which, definitely not as shiny or theoretically life-threatening as our previous topics, but really, really important. Last month, the bureau published a report that claimed to uncover evidence backing up President Donald Trump's claims that noncitizen voting cost him the 2020 election. He touted the report on True Social saying, "I won the election." This is, as you know, we've talked about this many times, one of Trump's favorite conspiracy theories. He cannot let it go. And WIRED reporters, Vittoria Elliott and David Gilbert, dug into how this specific report actually got made, who wrote it, and they discovered a lot of holes with this. I kind of want to start by saying, if you're listening to me and thinking, why do I care about a US Census Bureau report? They just do the census. They tell me how many people live in all of these different areas, how big families are, et cetera, et cetera. You're not 100 percent wrong, but this is really important data. These are reports about people and their lives, and the average citizen shouldn't have to know that much about it, but because of the situation we're in with the current administration, knowing these weird little intricacies of what's going on in government, I think has been really key to understanding the full picture here.

Brian Barrett: Also, to be clear, I do care.

Leah Feiger: You do care. There we go. All right. Can I run you through some of the quick down and dirty stuff, Brian, with what the report said?

Brian Barrett: Yes, please.

Leah Feiger: All right, great. So the report claims that out of over 128 million voter records analyzed, roughly 24,000 were tied to noncitizen status. To be clear, 24,000 might sound like a lot, but again, out of 128 million. These numbers are way too small to have changed the 2020 outcome, but they're still numbers. So when Tori and David went to experts about them, the experts actually said that they're more likely the product of data matching errors than actual noncitizens voting. So it was already this issue with the data themselves because the analysis combined so many disparate data sets. We're talking commercial voter files, immigration records, IRS, social security. WIRED has been reporting for a long time about how so many of these different agencies have had their work knitted together in the era of DOGE, in the era of Trump 2.0, and this is a good example of that. So this process is really error prone, and especially with commercial data, and you get false positives here rather than actual instances of noncitizen voting. What do you think about that, Brian?

Brian Barrett: Yeah, it all makes sense. And also, Leah, it's fair to say the amount of noncitizen voting that has been actually documented and found and prosecuted is vanishingly small.

Leah Feiger: Teeny tiny, like teeny, teeny tiny.

Brian Barrett: Which is not to say that there aren't some cases that get missed, but the idea that somehow there are 24,000 just sort of defies belief on the face of it. And yes, you can also see it makes total sense that as you're combining a bunch of databases, you are maybe double counting, you're maybe miscategorizing. This is a group that is not known to be particularly meticulous with the use of data. What I want to know, Leah, is how does this strike? Should I think of this as a preview of how this administration and the people around it will continue to sort of weaponize data and misconstrue data in and around the midterms and especially after the midterms if they don't like the results?

Leah Feiger: Great question. So you talk about the group that did this. I want to quickly hit that as we're getting into what the repercussions are. So the authors weren't listed on this report, which is crazy unusual, super, super unusual, hit up all sorts of red flags for our experts and former researchers at the US Census Bureau. Turns out WIRED was able to report for the first time that several of the reports authors have direct ties to the Trump administration and Republican political organizations.

Brian Barrett: No.

Leah Feiger: I know that shock of disbelief, it's crazy, but report authors include a former DOGE-affiliated attorney who's now at Commerce Department, a recent Census appointee who was previously at the Trump -aligned Claremont Institute, two staffers from the also Trump-aligned America First Policy Institute. So these aren't necessarily people who have had experience in this before. So when we're talking about impact on a larger scale, I think that we also have to really consider that some of these things, again, they appear on their face boring. An average citizen shouldn't be like, "Well, why do I care that this person is authoring this report? These are all just federal employees that I'm paying their salaries via my taxes, et cetera, et cetera." But obviously there is something like there appears to be political leanings here involved on these reports, and these reports have impact besides giving Trump and his administration credence to claims that the election was stolen. Census reports have to do with voting districts. It depends on who gets to vote going forward. And as we're getting into the midterms, the Census Bureau has been weighing in on this already in very weird and politicized ways that are very concerning to people in the room.

Brian Barrett: And obviously it's not just about this one report is institutions and individuals rely on Census Bureau data for so much outside of voting for so many things. And if you start to erode that trust and you start to say, "I don't know if I can believe these numbers full stop," that puts you in a really precarious position because there's no other source for Census Bureau data. It is a sort of singular entity.

Leah Feiger: Well, that's the thing, it's singular. And that's what I keep getting back to is when we're looking at this, even, I don't know, I'm thinking 20 years from now, but even 5, 10, 15 years from now, it's very hard to remove reports like this or remove bad data, faulty data from a government's memory. This is officially now official. I'm saying this incredibly eloquently, but in 10 years from now when they're like, "OK, so we have this data point from here, this data point from here, this is how we're constructing these different voting blocks and centers and et cetera," it's going to be really difficult to disentangle what the Trump administration has done. And I'm sure they know that. And so there's legacy here that we're going to have to be contending with for a really long time.

Brian Barrett: Coming up after the break, we'll share our WIRED/TIRED picks for the week. Stay with us.

Leah Feiger: It is time for our WIRED/TIRED segment. Whatever is new and cool is WIRED and whatever passé thing we're over is TIRED. Brian, tell me what you got.

Brian Barrett: Leah, my WIRED is technology that doesn't listen to you. I would love to normalize technology that isn't always recording just in case.

Leah Feiger: That feels outlandish, Brian. Is that part of our lives anymore?

Brian Barrett: Apparently not, because my TIRED, you'd be shocked to believe, relates to this. So Apple, in addition to its iPhones, announced two new Apple watches, the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. These watches come with, quote, "audio intelligence tools" that are powered by audio gathered by the watch's microphones. They include sound and music recognition, a conversation recap feature, a live rewind feature that lets you see a transcript of anything that was said nearby you in the last 15 seconds.

Leah Feiger: Oh my god.

Brian Barrett: I will say a couple things. One, this is an opt-in feature, so it's not automatically doing that. That's good. A lot of times these are opt-out, where it's like it's doing it when you don't even know it. My issue with this, as you might imagine, is that it's only opt-in for the person who's wearing the watch. If I'm standing around somebody who's wearing an Apple watch and they have this enabled and they're recording the last 15 seconds of our conversation and I don't know that, that's pretty frustrating. Don't love it.

Leah Feiger: That sucks. Bad. Bad all around.

Brian Barrett: Yeah. So I get that there are benefits to this. I get that there are circumstances and situations where I might even say, "Ooh, I wish I could Shazam that from my Apple watch. I forgot to ... " I don't know. I think these companies keep trying to balance the, "Here's this benefits that we can get from AI," but also you need to give so much to it to get those benefits and not just you, but the people around you. I don't know. I don't like that the default is increasingly becoming, "Hey, no, we're going to actually give this thing the ability to capture audio, video, whatever it is, of the world around you without the consent of the people who are being affected." That's it. That's my tired.

Leah Feiger: That's good. That makes sense. And just unlocking new fears every single day for me, Brian. Thank you.

Brian Barrett: That's what I do. That's what I'm here for.

Leah Feiger: OK. My WIRED is, happy back-to-school week for so many of my friends and their kids. It has been honestly incredibly cute to watch all these schools in my neighborhoods, in Brooklyn. Everyone's getting filled again. People are doing back-to-school shopping. It's incredibly adorable and feels wholesome and lovely, even in our unseasonably hot weather. Yeah, so I just like it, the changing of the seasons. It's nice.

Brian Barrett: Love that. My kids did go back to school the first week of August.

Leah Feiger: That's so crazy to me.

Brian Barrett: So I've been there. I've been in that world for a while already, but yes, congratulations to the Northeast for catching up.

Leah Feiger: My TIRED is a little bit sad though, which is there was a study that came out, I think it was sometime this week, maybe a day or two ago, about how US students, their reading scores have dropped, reached the lowest points that they have basically ever. And experts are saying this is because of screens and, quote, unquote, "digital distractions." I know that parents contend with this pretty consistently, but it was just a moment of we talk a lot on the pod about how these different technologies are impacting different groups. Is it worthwhile to regulate? Is it worthwhile to not? What does that actually entail? What does that really mean? And to just see it so starkly like, yeah, kids just aren't reading as much anymore. And this is post-Covid data, right? This is not counting what happened a couple years ago. So it was a moment where I was like, "Oh no. Will they be all right? Will the kids be all right?"

Brian Barrett: Yeah. A lot of them probably not, but some of them.

Zoë Schiffer: That's our show for today. We'll link to all the stories we spoke about in the show notes. Adriana Tapia produced this episode. It was mixed by Pran Bandi, who's also our New York studio engineer. It was fact-checked by Matt Giles and Daniel Roman. Kate Osborn is our executive producer, and Katie Drummond is WIRED's global editorial director.

entries.title: August 2026 Was the Hottest Month Ever Recorded: Copernicus Data
entries.summary: While the strengthening El Niño helped boost temperatures, climate change is the main culprit for making August so hot.
entries.content:
August was the planet’s hottest month ever recorded, capping a remarkably grim summer of heat records. With El Niño strengthening—and climate change continuing to heat things up—more records are likely in store well into next year.

Data from Copernicus, the European Union’s climate agency, shows that last month tied with July 2023 for Earth’s hottest month. (July is also usually the hottest month of the year.) This July also tied with July 2024 for the second-hottest July on record, while June 2026 was the second-hottest June ever recorded. The news comes on the heels of a separate announcement on Wednesday from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, which declared this was the hottest summer for the US, beating a previous record set during the Dust Bowl.

The sweltering summer is a grim sign of how burning fossil fuels is pushing temperatures up around the globe while unleashing more intense and longer heat waves.

“August 2026 was a remarkable month in the global climate record,” Samantha Burgess, the strategic lead for climate at the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, said in a statement. “Combined with record global sea surface temperatures and the warmest summer on record for Western Europe, these observations show how climate change is driving extremes across both the atmosphere and the oceans. The impacts of these conditions are increasingly being felt by communities, economies, and ecosystems across the world.”

The global average temperature for August was 1.65 degrees Celsius (3 degrees Fahrenheit) above the preindustrial average, according to Copernicus. While it was hot globally this summer, the impacts played out with dangerous and sometimes deadly results locally.

Researchers estimate that as many as 35,000 people died during heat waves in Germany, France, and Spain this summer. Record-breaking fires also raged across parts of Europe, unleashing the first documented fire cloud in France and threatening a key NASA observatory in Spain. In North America, wildfires in Canada and northern parts of the US filled areas across the Northeast with smoke.

Climate change has boosted background temperatures, but the El Niño roiling the eastern Pacific Ocean has piled on more heat. El Niños usually coincide with a temporary uptick in global temperature from 0.1 to 0.2 degrees Celsius. This year’s El Niño is forecast to reach record strength and upend weather around the globe. But the full impact on the planet’s temperature won’t be felt until next year, meaning that next summer may be even hotter than the one we just lived through.

Climate scientists have warned that the world needs to prevent long-term average warming from breaching 1.5 degrees Celsius to avoid the worst impacts of climate change. While temperatures above the threshold for a single month don’t represent a permanent breach of this temperature, they’re a sign that the world is getting closer to this benchmark.

Earlier this month, the UN warned in a report that the world is likely to cross the 1.5 degrees Celsius threshold in a few years. To slow and eventually reverse the rise in global temperatures, the world needs to stop burning fossil fuels and lower carbon emissions.

“This summer’s scorching heat, raging wildfires, and deadly floods are a warning of what lies ahead,” UN Secretary-General Antőnio Guterres said in a statement. “We must make the overshoot above 1.5 degrees as small and short as possible. That demands an overshoot of ambition.”

entries.title: Which iPhone 18 Model Should You Buy?
entries.summary: Apple’s new folding iPhone Duo is finally here, alongside refreshed Pro models. Our primer has all the details you need to choose the iPhone 18 that’s right for you.
entries.content:
With a fresh folding form factor, the new iPhone Duo is Apple’s most radical redesign in years. It lands alongside the more familiar-looking iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. There’s no regular iPhone 18, or at least, not yet. Rumors suggest we may see a more affordable base model, perhaps flanked by an iPhone 18e and a second-generation iPhone Air, in spring 2027.

The two new Pro iPhones are available to preorder on September 12 and ship on September 18. You can preorder the iPhone Duo from October 16, ahead of a full release on October 23. But which iPhone 18 model is right for you? I’ll break down the differences and what these phones have in common, so you can choose with confidence. For options beyond the iPhone 18 lineup, read our Best iPhones guide.

Why You Might Not Need to Upgrade

Before you drop all those hard-earned dollars, remember that you probably don’t need the latest iPhone. If you have an older iPhone, Apple does a good job of updating the software (the iPhone 11 Pro is still supported), and for hardware issues, your iPhone might be repairable; maybe it needs a battery replacement or these troubleshooting tips. Don’t feel like you have to spring for Apple’s shiny new thing.

Sadly, Apple raised iPhone Pro prices this year, so both models are $100 more expensive than the iPhone 17 Pro series.

If you’re set on upgrading, consider raising funds by selling your old iPhone. Just be sure to back up your iPhone, and factory reset it before you sell or give it away. Once the new device arrives, we have tips on how to set up your new iPhone and what settings to change to get the most out of it.

Which iPhone 18 Is Right for You?

We’ll start by looking at what’s the same across the iPhone 18 models this year.

All three new iPhones have Apple’s A20 Pro chip inside, and, you guessed it, this is Apple’s most powerful chip ever. Now, iPhones are already the most capable phones for raw compute power, but the A20 Pro promises a significant jump in performance (around 20 percent faster and 30 percent more efficient than the last generation). It also packs a new neural engine to power on-device AI and a new thermal design with a larger vapor chamber to keep things cool. For the iPhone Duo, the A20 Pro has a display engine to ensure smooth transitions between two screens. While Apple doesn’t list the RAM, every model is rumored to have 12 GB.

While they come in different sizes and the Duo has two, every iPhone features an OLED screen that Apple calls a Super Retina XDR display. They also have ProMotion technology, otherwise known as a 120-Hz refresh rate. These adaptive refresh rates can drop as low as 1 Hz when there's little activity on the screen, enabling features like the always-on display without draining the battery too much.

The displays are protected by the scratch-resistant and antireflective Ceramic Shield 2, the same as last year’s iPhone 17 range. And they can go from 1 nit up to 3,000 nits of brightness. Only the iPhone Duo has a custom nano-texture finish on the interior screen, giving it a matte look that’s designed to reduce glare and crease visibility.

All the phones have an IP68 rating for water and dust resistance, meaning they can survive a short dunk in fresh water. They all come in four storage options (256 GB, 512 GB, 1 TB, or 2 TB), support Qi2 magnetic wireless charging (MagSafe), USB-C 3.2, Dual SIM, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, and Ultra-Wideband (UWB). It also has Siri AI, Apple Intelligence, Emergency SOS via Satellite, and Crash Detection.

To help you better understand which model to buy, here's precisely where they diverge.

Apple has taken its time with its first foldable, enabling it to learn from the best folding phones already on the market. Eschewing the more prevalent book- and flip-style foldables, Apple has gone with a passport-sized form factor for the iPhone Duo, similar to Samsung's recent Galaxy Z Fold8 (our current favorite). The Duo has a 5.4-inch screen on the outside, but unfolds to reveal a 7.6-inch display inside that feels like an iPad Mini.

The iPhone Duo has a tough titanium frame, a precision hinge with magnets for that satisfying snap-shut, and an IP68 rating for solid dust and water resistance. But at 254 grams and 11.3 mm thick when folded, and 5.2 mm unfolded, the Duo is not the slimmest or lightest foldable around (the Fold8 is 201 grams, 9.7 mm thick folded, and 4.5 mm unfolded).

Foldables don’t have as much space for cameras, so the Duo drops Face ID (Touch ID is in the side power button instead) and makes do without a telephoto lens (you get a 48-megapixel primary camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide). But it has room for the biggest-ever iPhone battery, promising 24 hours of mixed use.

Where Apple will likely add a lot of value to the foldable phone category is with its software design. Controls have been pushed to the side and stacked vertically to free up more screen real estate. Apps offer plenty of split-screen support, and transitions between displays look slick. Apple has also included features that take advantage of the fact that you can prop the Duo open on a table or nightstand, so there’s StandBy support to use the outer screen as an alarm clock, while the inside display gently pulses with light to wake you.

Who it’s for: You want something different. You’re curious about folding phones or already convinced they’re great and can’t wait to experience Apple’s take.

The iPhone 18 Pro is similar to last year’s 17 Pro, with a 6.3-inch display, though the Dynamic Island has been slightly slimmed and can now show three Live Activities notifications at once. It keeps the same aluminum unibody, with Ceramic Shield on the back glass, Ceramic Shield 2 on the front, and an IP68 rating. Black is back, and there’s also a new Burgundy color, alongside Glacier and Silver. Those colors look more uniform than the 17 Pro’s two-tone finish.

Two standout upgrades stand out: The new A20 Pro chipset is faster and more power-efficient, and the main camera now has a variable aperture. The A20 Pro also enables better on-device AI and is aided by a redesigned vapor chamber to keep it cool while it works. Apple reckons you can expect 34 hours of video playback; that’s three hours more than the 17 Pro.

The camera introduces a physical lens aperture. Like the pupil of your eye, the aperture is the lens opening that lets light in. A bigger aperture can let in more light for better photos when it’s darker, and a smaller aperture can help you avoid overly bright photos when the sun is shining. But the aperture also impacts depth of field, so a bigger aperture can help you achieve that bokeh blurred background effect for a portrait photo, while a smaller aperture can help retain detail across a wider landscape shot. The camera app has new features and controls to help you take advantage of it.

Who it’s for: You don't want a big phone, but you want full-strength Apple silicon, a top camera, and all the latest features.

If foldables aren’t for you, the iPhone 18 Pro Max offers the biggest screen you can get at 6.9 inches, and it is a battery-life beast. Apple says you can get up to 43 hours of video playback out of a full charge; that’s a six-hour increase on last year’s already impressive 17 Pro Max. It has the same design and colors as the regular Pro, just bigger.

You also get the new chip and variable aperture camera. Both Pro models now boast a versatile triple 48-megapixel camera system with pro controls for lens aperture, shutter speed, and white balance. The class-leading video capture goes up to 4K at 120 fps. The iPhone 18 Pro phones are the right pick for photographers and videographers.

Who it’s for: You want the best Apple has to offer, including a big screen and long battery life, in a familiar form factor.

How to Get the iPhone 18 Unlocked

It makes sense to buy your iPhone unlocked, since it's much easier to switch carriers or use an international eSIM when you travel. The iPhones sold through Apple's storefront are unlocked, so Apple.com is the best place to buy them. During a preorder period, you can only purchase a newly announced iPhone from Apple.

Don't forget to take advantage of Apple's promotions: You get three free months of Apple One, which includes Apple Music, Apple TV+, Apple Arcade, News+, Apple Fitness+, and extra iCloud storage. Just watch out, because it will auto-bill you after the trial. Set a reminder to cancel if you don't want to continue subscribing to these services.

  • The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 for 256 GB
  • The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199 for 256 GB
  • The iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299 for 256 GB

Apple has some financing options. If you have an Apple Card, you can pay for your iPhone over 24 months at 0-percent APR, and most carriers offer financing deals, too. Apple also offers Apple Upgrade, enabling you to lease your new iPhone from $35 a month for 24 months for the entry-model iPhone 18 Pro (12 months starts at $50 a month). We don’t think it’s a good deal, but if you’re tempted, remember you must return it in good condition (AppleCare+ with Theft and Loss costs an extra $15 a month).

entries.title: Best Robot Lawn Mowers (2026): 12+ Models Tested Over 3 Years
entries.summary: Smart mowers are an expensive alternative to old-fashioned yard work, but they’re finally good enough to consider if you’d rather sip an iced tea and watch a robot tame your lawn.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

Lawn care is a monotonous, thankless task. Who wants to mow the lawn when you could be lollygagging in a hammock with a cold drink, watching a robot do it for you? That’s right: no one. Robot lawn mowers were once the preserve of the wealthy, and yes, they can still be on the pricey side. But they’re getting cheaper and better all the time.

I’ve tested a handful of the best robot lawn mowers over the past three years, and after comparing a fresh crop this mowing season, I'm delighted to tell you that robot mowers are actually good now. I've got some recommendations, honorable mentions, and a list of robot mowers you should avoid. Read on for everything you need to know about lawn-tending bots.

Updated September 2026: I added mowers from Roborock, Segway, Eufy, and Sunseeker, added information about night mowing to the FAQ, and updated prices.

Other Robot Mowers I Tested and Liked

Roborock Rockmow X120H Lidar for $3,200: Better known for its robot vacuums, Roborock also makes robot mowers, and the X120H Lidar is its flagship model (discounted to a far more reasonable $2,000 at the time of writing). I actually tested the UK model, the identical Z120 Lidar (£2,299). This mower employs Lidar and AI vision, so it can cut without satellite connections, with no RTK antenna required. It also supports 4G and comes with a 3-year data plan. It is Four Wheel Drive (4WD) and has ingenious front wheels that pivot and turn independently to navigate tight areas smoothly, with minimal churning of your lawn. There’s a single disc underneath with six cutting blades and a reasonably wide, 9.5-inch (24 cm) cutting width. It supports a 0.8 to 2.7-inch (20 to 70 mm) cutting height, can cover up to around 21,500 square feet, and, most impressively, can handle an 80 percent (up to 39-degree) slope. A full charge gives you 110 minutes of mowing time, and it takes around 50 minutes to charge.

After some minor setup hassles (battery error), the Rockmow Z120 has impressed me. It looks to be the most capable mower I have tested yet for navigating uneven terrain. Apparently, it can automatically create maps, but it defaulted to the manual mode for me, prompting me to remote control it around the borders of my lawn. Edge mowing is the big disappointment, with the mower regularly leaving a strip on one edge of my lawn. I’m not keen on the optional PreciEdge Module (£150) that promises to reduce edges to 3 cm. I haven’t tested it, but feel it should be included in a mower this expensive. Why is it optional? Who doesn’t want their edges properly cut? It avoided most obstacles just fine, but was occasionally oversensitive, avoiding plants swaying over the border edge. The Rain Protection mode is a little too sensitive, preventing the mower from starting several hours after rain, so I had to override it. It also lacks a Spot Mode, though it is so heavy I would not want to carry it between lawn areas. I think this design, with the rotating wheels, has real potential if Roborock can improve the AI/software. Unfortunately, it's not currently available in the US right now, but hopefully be back in stock soon since it was released just this past summer.

Eufy Robot Lawn Mower E15 for $1,300: This is another wire-free mower that uses a camera system to automatically map lawns and avoid obstacles. It’s very similar to my top pick and also has a super handy Spot Mode that lets you drop and mow on unmapped areas. But even after a big price drop from its original RRP, it’s still more expensive than the TerraMow, and it’s not as good at cutting edges. It can cover up to 0.2 acres (8,700 square feet), cut from 1 to 3 inches, and handle up to 18-degree slopes. It is also fairly quiet and has GPS tracking, but you must have Wi-Fi coverage in your backyard, or you'll need a 4G data subscription. I found the setup lengthy due to a firmware download, but the mapping and the first cut were decent. Object avoidance is very good. The E15 can only run during the day and doesn't cope very well with inclines. I also found it frequently failed to cut the edges of the lawn and doesn't perform well if the grass is damp. The more affordable Eufy C15 (£999) is very similar, but designed for smaller lawns (up to 5,300 square feet) and only available in the UK and Europe right now.

It kept my back lawn neat without issues, but my front lawn has a dip and ill-defined border that it struggled with. That said, every time it looked as though it might get stuck, it managed to maneuver out of trouble. There’s a dial to adjust mowing height for the C15, whereas you can do it in the app with the E15. Both come with a covered charging base, which often costs extra with rivals. If you’re interested, watch out for a sale event (I’ve seen the E15 drop below $1,000, which makes it far more tempting).

Segway Navimow X430 for $2,249: My backyard is both a Wi-Fi and 5G dead zone. Before manually mowing the yard I save all my podcasts and music to offline mode, and I let my fiancee know she’ll need to deploy a carrier pigeon if she needs to get my attention. So, it was a relief to see just how quickly the navigation system of the Navimow X430 recognized the unit across the treacherous triple lot that surrounds my house. It connected within seconds of beginning the initial setup and 20 minutes later, the robot mower was on its way using the handy auto-mapping function. As it turns out, I didn't need the three beers I'd brought with me when I embarked upon this process, assuming it would be on par with the weeks-long headache it took to get the Mammotion Luba 2 connected and operational last summer.

It did an above-average job on its first pass despite the endless flurry of compost piles, stray bushes, fencing and detritus from half-finished gardening projects that litter my half-acre lawn, though I opted for manual mapping to take advantage of its aptitude at hugging the wobbly brick borders of some raised beds with relative ease. The sites claims that it can handle “tall, thick and dense grass," which I had the perfect scenario to test. After a two weeks of dealing with an endless cycle of torrential downpours and blistering heat, I was left with few open windows for a good mow before my patchy, crabby grass got too unwieldy for the Navimow’s 4-inch height maximum. I watched with disappointment as it casually drove over some stray blades that went to seed without making any impact whatsoever. Despite that, the Navimow X430 has impressed me with its ease-of-use. We'll update our impressions here with additional testing, but so far so good.—Pete Cottell

Sunseeker X7 Gen 2 Wireless Robot Lawn Mower for $2,700: If you have a large, challenging lawn, this could be a mower worth considering. It combines built-in NET-RTK, GPS, and AI vision, has floating dual disc blades for uneven terrain, and can work at night thanks to an Indirect Time of Flight camera. It is also all-wheel drive (AWD) and can handle 70 percent slopes up to 35 degrees. It can cover more than 32,000 square feet. I love the wide 14-inch cutting width, the relatively quiet operation (it never went over 60 decibels but was usually even quieter), even though I’d advise against mowing at night because of the risk to wildlife. Sadly, the automatic mapping was mediocre, and there’s no Spot Mode for a drop-and-mow. This Gen 2 mower brings a raft of improvements over the original, including night vision, faster processing, enhanced durability and traction, a built-in screen, and onboard RTK without a separate antenna. But only the original Sunseeker X7 ($2,700) is available to buy on Amazon. You currently have to go through a dealer to get the Gen 2.

Husqvarna Aspire R6V for £999: While the reliable Husqvarna 410XE Nera was my top pick for a long time, you can get more affordable mowers now, without the hassle of RTK antennas. The Husqvarna Aspire R6V is just such a mower. It uses a combination of GPS and AI vision with a camera on the front. It was easy to set up and map the lawn in the app, but you will need a good Wi-Fi signal across your yard for it to work effectively. I was a little disappointed in the sensitive obstacle avoidance, as it left large uncut strips around the edges of my lawn. I was able to reduce the verge a little with some tinkering, but it was still larger than the recommendations above. Note: This model is currently not available in the US.

Anthbot Genie 3000 for $900: This often-discounted mower was my budget pick for a while, but mowers have moved on, so you can get better performance without the satellite antenna now. It offers auto-mapping, but the remote-control option works better. The mower cut my lawn effectively, but even after repeated map updates, it left an uncut verge. The obstacle avoidance works well, and it cuts in neat lines. It had no issues returning to charge or following a schedule. The voice that says it has connected or started mowing began to annoy me, but thankfully, it can be turned off. There were some glitches with rain alerts that prevented it from mowing, even long after the rain had stopped. I also experienced some flaky connection issues with the GPS, and it occasionally got stuck. While there is support for multiple areas, the mower often struggled picking up a signal in my front yard. Ultimately, this is still a decent mower when discounted, provided you have a modest-sized, straightforward lawn.

Mova Lidax 2000 for $1,199: With a sleek design and a mixture of 360-degree lidar for 3D mapping and a camera with AI vision, this mower proved very effective. Setup was straightforward, and there’s no need for wires or an antenna, though I did have to adjust the map manually. You can set multiple areas, and its navigation is generally very good. It mowed in neat lines, successfully avoided thin posts for the badminton net and other obstacles, and completed an excellent edge pass at the end. With some of the closest edge mowing I’ve seen, I was all set to recommend this mower, but then it got stuck. A couple of times, it seemed to be stuck, then managed to free itself, but an uneven problem spot proved to be its nemesis, and it chewed up a patch of grass trying to get free. Eventually, I had to make that spot a no-go zone. This mower is still worth considering, particularly if you see it on sale; just be prepared to tweak the map. The 2000 covers up to half an acre. If you have a quarter of an acre or less, the Mova Lidax 1000 ($1,299) is much cheaper but has the same features.

Avoid These Mowers

Stiga A6V: I like that this mower only needs the charging station and has no need for an antenna. The buggy setup was my first red flag, as a firmware update failed and had to be repeated. Once up and running, I found the mower always left a big verge, even after adjustment. The AI vision camera is very slow to react to obstacles and not very good at navigating around them. It hit the ball several times in my test, and I had to hit the stop button as it got too close to my cat. It lacks useful features like automapping and spot-mow, and there are better options for the money above. The yellow finish is a bit garish for my tastes too.

EcoFlow Blade: While it was easy to set up and cut my lawn nicely without the need for any boundary wire, the EcoFlow Blade sometimes struggled with GPS navigation and ended up stuck in a flower bed. It also left an untouched strip around the edge of my lawn. The object avoidance was solid, and it can be automated in the app, though it occasionally failed to start a scheduled cut for me. EcoFlow seems to have discontinued this model, though it is still on sale in Europe. Probably best to avoid.

Yardcare E400: Curious about the budget end of the robot mower market, I agreed to try the Yardcare E400, but this mower was an unmitigated disaster from start to finish. It’s a boundary wire model, so you must run wire around the area you want mowed. Yardcare suggests it can cover up to 4,300 square feet and cut grass between 0.8 and 2.4 inches. The problem is that it gets stuck frequently and struggles to even get on and off its charging station reliably. After trying multiple fixes to no avail and going through customer support, I had to conclude that this model has a serious design flaw.

How Do Robot Lawn Mowers Work?

Perhaps counterintuitively, the setup instructions for your robot lawn mower will likely tell you to start by cutting the grass. Robot mowers mostly can’t deal with long grass. Unlike traditional mowers, these robots don’t collect grass cuttings; they mulch instead, and they are designed to cut frequently, keeping your lawn short and simply leaving the cuttings on the ground, which can also improve lawn health. Most robot mowers are designed to run two or three times a week during the growing season (from late spring to early fall).

They have rechargeable batteries onboard and can last from half an hour to several hours on a full charge. They return to the charging base and recharge automatically when their power runs low. Most mowers have simple controls, a small display, and an emergency stop button. You can generally start and stop mowing, set schedules, and create or edit mapped areas using the onboard controls or the companion mobile app, very much like a robot vacuum.

What Features Should I Look For in a Robot Mower?

There are many factors to consider in choosing a robot mower, and the best choice for you often depends on your yard.

Robot lawn mowers are generally rated to cover a specific square footage, with wider coverage requiring models with larger batteries. Alongside yard size, you should consider the shape and topography of your lawn, as most robot mowers will struggle with steep inclines. While you can often map out separate areas so your robot mower can mow front and back lawns, for example, it will generally need you to lift and carry it between those areas. If you have an uneven garden or steep slopes, look for a four-wheel-drive (4WD) or all-wheel-drive (AWD) mower and check the manufacturer's rating for inclines.

There are a few types of navigation that robot mowers employ. We’ve tested five different approaches, though some mowers combine multiple technologies for better performance.

  • Satellite: Often employing something called Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) Global Positioning System (GPS), these mowers need a satellite signal to navigate and will have a receiver that must be placed in the open with a clear line of sight to the sky. Satellite navigation mowers are not suitable for areas with tall trees or buildings.
  • Light Detection and Ranging (lidar): This technology sends out rapid laser pulses to 3D map the terrain (it is also used by self-driving cars). It enables mowers to cut grass under thick tree canopies or near tall buildings where GPS signals usually fail.
  • Cameras: Cameras and onboard AI are used for obstacle detection and avoidance. AI vision can automatically map areas and cut the grass while avoiding obstacles it encounters, much like how most robot vacuums navigate a home to clean the floors.
  • Wire boundary: These mowers require you to install a perimeter wire as a boundary around your lawn that marks out the border the mower should not cross. It's a messy job that can be tricky.
  • Remote control: You mow your lawn from the comfort of your home using a remote controller or an app on your phone. Some only work via remote control, while others can also cut automatically.

Robot mowers generally come with large charging docks, and you’ll need to earmark a suitable spot for yours. They usually have extensive weatherproof cabling, but you will have to find a route to an outdoor socket.

To connect to your mower and schedule a mow, update the firmware, or remote control it where supported, you need a decent Wi-Fi signal or a Bluetooth connection. It’s best to set up your mower’s charging station within range of your Wi-Fi network. Some mowers also need a strong Wi-Fi signal to operate effectively, so you might consider adding an outdoor mesh router. If you want to connect your phone via Bluetooth, you will have to get quite close.

How Noisy Are Robot Mowers?

Most robot mowers are far quieter than their traditional counterparts. You can expect them to operate at around 55 decibels, though they may go as high as 75 decibels. We only tested battery-powered mowers, but expect gas mowers to be louder. While the operation is often quiet, I did find that several mowers made annoying beeping sounds when backing up or had a loud recorded voice during setup or upon receiving a command.

Do Robot Mowers Work in Any Weather?

Robot mowers and their charging stations usually have IP ratings and can cope with rain, but you should pack up and bring your mower indoors during the winter months. Many robot mowers have some kind of rain sensor and will pause mowing when it gets too wet. Some mowers may need to be paused manually. The wheels can churn up your lawn and get caked in mud if mowers continue to labor in the rain, especially with larger and heavier models.

How Well Do Robot Mowers Cut?

Mowers of different sizes will have varying cutting widths, denoting the width of the strip they can cut on each pass. Most also have floating cutting decks that enable you to choose the length of grass you want (typically 1 to 3 inches). Many robot mowers seem to struggle with cutting around the edges of a lawn, especially if there’s a wall or fence that prevents them from getting close enough.

It’s common to find an uncut verge around the edge of your lawn, so you might need to occasionally get the string trimmer out. Every robot mower I’ve tested has also struggled to cut the area around the charging station, so I recommend placing the unit on a deck or pavement if possible.

Can I Install a Robot Mower Myself?

​Yes, most robot mowers can be installed by anyone, but you might want to set aside an afternoon to work out any snags. Finding the best spot for the receiver for a satellite mower can be tricky. The mapping process can also take a while; usually, the mower will prompt you to remote-control it around the border you want to set. After the first mow, you should review its performance and make tweaks to ensure it’s covering the entire area you want to cut.

Can Robot Mowers Mow at Night?

Some models are capable of mowing at night in the dark using headlights, Lidar, and Time of Flight sensors, alongside their usual navigation capabilities. This can be convenient and also removes the risk for pets or children playing on the lawn during the day. However, there is a risk of injuring nocturnal wildlife, like hedgehogs in the UK and Europe. Mowers are also more likely to make mistakes and get stuck in the dark. It may be better to schedule mowing for dawn or dusk.

How I Test Robot Lawn Mowers

I test each robot lawn mower for at least a month, on at least two different lawn areas, assessing the ease of setup, the mapping process, automatic scheduling (where available), navigation, obstacle avoidance, and the quality of the final cut, looking for length, uniformity, and any missed patches. Where applicable, I try extra features, tweak settings in the app, and check how the mower handles different weather conditions. I also keep an eye on battery performance and charging time to ensure it aligns with the manufacturer's claims.
